catalog_quote: Seri, a language isolate spoken in northwestern Mexico, regularly assigns stress to the penultimate syllable of a root; affixes are not relevant for determining the placement of stress. A heavy final syllable in the root attracts stress, however, although a final consonant is extrametrical. ... Some roots have extrametrical final syllables and a few roots have exceptional stress. ... The stress pattern is affected by the weight of a syllable. When the last syllable in the domain has a long vowel, a diphthong, or a complex coda, that syllable is stressed. ... the final consonant does not contribute to the syllable weight for this purpose ... final consonant is extrametrical (Hayes 1982, Hayes 1995). sweep_summary: Seri (seri1257) search: two title hits, both by Marlett and both the same analysis. (1) Marlett 2008 (Linguistic Discovery 6.1, the catalog's deciding source) was already. re-read and copied to our check folder; it confirms the 'weight' coding verbatim (root-domain moraic trochee, penultimate default, heavy final attracts stress, final C extrametrical, lexical extrametrical syllables, exceptions). (2) Marlett 2006 'El acento, la extrametricalidad y la palabra mínima en seri' (Santa Rosa conference proceedings, Spanish) was not yet obtained; downloaded live from lengamer.org (HTTP 200, 9-pp text-layer PDF, logged). It is the Spanish original that 2008 expands: same rule, same examples, explicitly restricted to nouns and without the phonetics/audio section -> 'refines' (confirms coding; earlier, narrower scope). Nothing to acquire; no priority items. The catalog's deciding source (2008) stands; 2006 should be added to the per-language bibliography as its antecedent.

new_statements.quote: Los siguientes ejemplos muestran que el acento normalmente cae en la penúltima sílaba de palabras multisilábicas. ... Cuando la última sílaba tiene una vocal larga o una coda compleja, esta sílaba (generalmente) atrae el acento. Por lo tanto, sabemos que seri es una lengua sensible a la cantidad ... Entonces propongo que la última consonante es extrametrical ... he propuesto que el acento en los sustantivos se basa en un pie trocaico construido al lado derecho de la raíz. La última consonante de la raíz no cuenta para este propósito. La última sílaba es pesada solamente si tiene dos vocales (o más) en el núcleo o dos consonantes (o más) en la coda.
new_statements.translation: The following examples show that stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words. ... When the last syllable has a long vowel or a complex coda, that syllable (generally) attracts stress. So we know Seri is a quantity-sensitive language ... I therefore propose that the final consonant is extrametrical ... I have proposed that stress in nouns is based on a trochaic foot built at the right edge of the root. The final consonant of the root does not count for this purpose. The final syllable is heavy only if it has two (or more) vowels in the nucleus or two (or more) consonants in the coda.

new_statements.quote: 1.3. Acentuación. En general, la primera vocal de la raíz es la vocal acentuada.d Hay muchas excepciones, sin embargo, sobre todo en los sustantivos. Generalmente en la literatura seri no se usa acento ortográfico. En este diccionario, sin embargo, se lo ha utilizado para ayudar al lector a saber cuándo el acento no cae en la primera sílaba de la palabra. [note d, p. 940:] En ciertas secuencias de vocales que empiezan con o, como oa, oaa, y oii, el acento tiende a moverse fonéticamente a la segunda vocal de la secuencia, como en coáatjö dulce (raíz –oaatjö), coáan turbio (raíz –oaan) y coíij tubular (raíz –oiij). El acento no se mueve en ciertas palabras, como canóaa panga y cöcacóaat enseñar.
new_statements.translation: 1.3. Stress. In general, the first vowel of the root is the stressed vowel. There are many exceptions, however, above all among nouns. Generally no orthographic accent is used in Seri literature. In this dictionary, however, it has been used to help the reader know when the stress does not fall on the first syllable of the word. [note d, p. 940:] In certain vowel sequences beginning with o, such as oa, oaa and oii, the stress tends to move phonetically to the second vowel of the sequence, as in coáatjö 'sweet' (root -oaatjö), coáan 'turbid' (root -oaan) and coíij 'tubular' (root -oiij). The stress does not move in certain words, such as canóaa 'boat' and cöcacóaat 'to teach'.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog's record for Seri (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule field, and its existing statement (Marlett 2006, same as Marlett 2008 held by the project) codes Seri as weight-sensitive within the root: root-penult by default, root-final if heavy, with extrametricality. The dictionary sketch instead states the older root-initial formulation ('la primera vocal de la raíz es la vocal acentuada'), i.e. a morphological root rule with 'many exceptions'. This is a different rule type (root-initial vs. quantity-sensitive right edge of the root), so it is logged as a contradiction, but it is the SAME author's earlier analysis: Marlett 2008 (p. 3-4, held by the project) quotes it as rule (3) fr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the first vowel (syllable) of the root, not of the word: prefixes are unstressed, so stress position within the word depends on the morphology. Many lexical exceptions, especially nouns. Supporting details: long vowels occur only in stressed syllables (p. 825); the consonant after the stressed vowel is strengthened/lengthened, a pattern absent in most Spanish loans (p. 26; tech note a p. 940); in true compounds the main stress is on the last member (p. 838); in o-initial vowel sequences (oa, oaa, oii) stress shifts phonetically to the second vowel except in some words (note d, p. 940).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described. The sketch speaks of 'acento primario' (aamóo xah, p. 825) and 'acento principal' in compounds (p. 838), implying a non-primary prominence on the other member, but gives no rule for secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Hay muchas excepciones, sobre todo en los sustantivos' (p. 828); phonetic stress shift in oa/oaa/oii sequences with lexical exceptions canóaa, cöcacóaat (note d, p. 940); compounds stress the last member (p. 838); postpositions with an overt complement lack strong prosodic stress while bare postpositions often carry it (p. 878); most auxiliary words have no prosodic stress, ihi does (p. 879); the 'halx' infix -a- shifts stress to the next syllable and lengthens the vowel (entry -a, -a-, p. 28); loanwords lack post-tonic consonant lengthening (p. 26).
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary describes the Seri of the Comcáac community (Sonora, Mexico: El Desemboque and Punta Chueca), treated as one language; p. 825 fn. 1 notes only minor inter-speaker variation (e.g. j for x word-initially in some words). No dialect split is described, and the loan/exception remarks concern the same variety. Marlett 2006/2008 describe the same variety.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, within the same author's work. The dictionary's grammar sketch (Moser & Marlett 2005, sect. 1.3 p. 828) gives the root-initial rule 'the first vowel of the root is the stressed vowel' with 'many exceptions, above all among nouns'. Marlett 2006 (Spanish) and Marlett 2008 (Linguistic Discovery), both already held by the project in the seri1257 custody folder and the latter the catalog's deciding source, restate that rule as Marlett 1981's rule (3), say it has many exceptions, and replace it with a quantity-sensitive right-edge rule computed on the root (penult by default, final if the root-final syllable is heavy, with a single final consonant extrametrical and some lexically extrametrical syllables). The later analysis supersedes the dictionary's; the data are largely the same, and for one- and two-syllable roots both rules select the same syllable. Both sources agree that the domain is the root (prefixes never take stress), that long vowels appear only in stressed syllables, and that the post-tonic consonant is lengthened. The catalog's empty rule field should be filled with the weight-sensitive-in-root rule per Marlett 2008, with the dictionary cited as the root-initial formulation it replaced.

sources.quote: 8. Stress. Primary stress is predictable to a high degree, stress usually falling on the first vowel of the stem. It may be shifted by later rules to prefix vowels, however, as we have seen in (108) above. Some verbs that do not fit into this pattern are the result of the reanalysis of prefix material. [...] Not all verbs with stress on the second syllable of the stem are so easily analyzed. Compare the following forms. (111) /-mošíme/ be drunk; /-moképe/ be sick; /-motóman/ be weak. The significance of the sequence mo- is unknown. [p. 143:] There is more surface irregularity with nouns since many were probably compounds or derived nouns historically. Moser and Moser (1965:56) claimed that stress was phonemic on the basis of the following type of data. My analysis is given on the right. (112) ʔípxaš my nephew /ʔi-apxaš/ → ʔi-ápxaš → ʔí-pxaš; ʔipxáš our flesh /ʔi-pxaš/ → ʔi-pxáš

sources.quote: On the word level, stress generally occurs on the leftmost syllable of the root. The presence of various kinds of affixes does not affect the placement of stress. [...] (8) An unstressed syllable cannot contain a complex nucleus. [...] As far as word-level phonology is concerned, a complex nucleus is found only in the primary stressed syllable of the word. Or, to state it in reverse, stress is never assigned to a syllable with a simple nucleus if the root contains a syllable with a complex nucleus. Stress is therefore assigned to the leftmost syllable of the root unless another syllable in the root contains a complex nucleus (or if stress is lexically marked).
